title: Contractor or employee is not just a label

sources.claim: Whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor depends on the actual working relationship (economic reality), not on the label in a contract. The federal rule has changed several times since 2021; in February 2026 the Department of Labor PROPOSED replacing the 2024 rule (a proposal, not a final rule), and states may use stricter tests, so current federal and state rules must be checked.

sections.skill: Recognize that worker classification depends on the real relationship

questions.prompt: What decides whether a worker is an employee or contractor?

choices.text: Only what the worker prefers to be called
Only the size of the paycheck
Only the title written in the contract

questions.intro: Whether a worker is an EMPLOYEE or an INDEPENDENT CONTRACTOR depends on the actual working relationship, not on the label in a contract. Factors often include how much control the business has over how and when the work is done, whether the worker can profit or lose based on their own decisions, whether they work for other clients, who provides tools, and whether the work is ongoing. Federal rules have changed several times, and states may use stricter tests. Misclassification can bring back taxes and penalties, so check current rules or ask a professional.

questions.prompt: A "cat" sign on a dog does what?

choices.text: Makes it a cat in the eyes of the law

questions.intro: If you put a sign saying "cat" on a dog, it still barks. Writing "independent contractor" on a contract does not change the work if the business sets the hours, provides the tools, trains the worker and directs every step. Rules look at what the relationship is really like, the same way you would look at the animal rather than the sign.
